title: Higher-Order Certified Robustness for Regression
claim: Using gradient information shifts the certified-radius distribution well beyond the state-of-the-art baseline, consistently across two tasks.
layout: 2 stacked panels, top-to-bottom, CDF curves with dotted median lines
description: Two vertically stacked line plots show cumulative distribution functions of certified radius. Panel (a), MNIST rotation, has x from 0 to 0.3 pixels. Panel (b), UTKFace age estimation, has x from 0 to 2.5. Each panel has three curves: a solid teal curve for (E,C)+M, a solid magenta curve for (E,C,G)+M, which adds gradients, and a dashed orange curve for alpha-smoothing. Faint dotted vertical lines mark each curve's median or mean. In both panels the magenta curve sits furthest right, so its radii are largest. The orange baseline is spread out and has mass near zero. The teal curve is steep and narrow. A legend in the lower right lists each method's success probability and sigma. Bold titles sit above the plots, with captions (a) and (b) below.
caption: CDFs of certified radii using the best fixed configuration for each method. Panel (a) compares methods on MNIST rotation; panel (b) evaluates the aperiodic UTKFace age-estimation task. In both panels, the x-axis reports certified radius in pixels, meaning the ℓ2 perturbation norm in normalized pixel space. All methods use success probability 0.9.
abstract: Randomized smoothing has emerged as a scalable technique for certifying the adversarial robustness of classifiers. However, its application to regression remains under-explored and faces unique challenges. Existing regression certificates rely on probabilistic acceptance regions and fail to exploit the local geometry of the function. In this work, we present a novel framework for certified robust regression that addresses these limitations. We derive a prediction-centered certificate that guarantees the stability of the smoothed model's prediction and ensures practical computability at test time. We investigate several alternatives for constructing these certificates by explicitly incorporating means, variances, and gradients. In particular, we demonstrate on the MNIST rotation task that utilizing gradient information yields significantly tighter robustness certificates compared to the current state-of-the-art, alpha-smoothing.
